newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore exports rally as electronic demand rises.
newsitem.headline: Singapore exports rally as electronic demand rises.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports bounced back into the black in December thanks to a recovery in the key electronics industry, a Reuters poll of economists suggested on Thursday.

Fifteen financial institutions, surveyed between Tuesday and Thursday, produced an average forecast of a rise of 2.9 percent year-on-year in nominal terms in the island's non-oil domestic exports. This compares with a fall of 8.8 percent in November and a rise of 1.1 percent in October.

Economists said the export recovery in December was due to a turnaround in the global electronics market, which absorbs about half Singapore's industrial production and produces almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.

"December's export figures will be a lot better than November's," said Liew Yin Sze, economist at brokerage J.M. Sassoon. "But there won't be any sharp recovery soon. I expect a full recovery to only come in April or May."
Wholesale demand for electronics products and computer components plunged in the third quarter of 1996 with many U.S. and Asian high techology companies reducing orders.
This translated into slower economic growth for Singapore, which official figures show dipped to 6.5 percent last year from 8.8 percent growth in 1995.
Economists said the electronics slump was mainly a cyclical downturn sparked by inventory surpluses, and they forecast demand for electronics would recover strongly worldwide by mid-1997.
But they said the first quarter of this year might still see further bad months for Asian electronics producers until the recovery gets properly under way.

"The improvement in December exports should not be taken as an indication of a sustainable recovery in Singapore's manufacturing sector," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS/Standard & Poors, in Singapore.
Standard Chartered Bank's regional economist, Tan Swee Liang, agreed and said January's export data could see a return to year-on-year declines.
"Especially next month, you will probably see a fall again because January 1996 showed very strong export growth," she said.
"On a cyclical basis, Singapore economic growth saw a trough in the third quarter of 1996 and won't finally see a pick up until the second quarter of this year."

Economists said U.S. electronics demand reached a low point in August or September and expected a time lag of six to seven months before this cyclical low-point was passed back along the supply chain to Asian primary producers.

The same Reuters poll produced an average forecast of a rise of 1.5 percent year-on-year in December in Singapore's consumer price index of inflation. The index rose 1.4 percent year-on-year in November.
Singapore's official export figures and CPI data are due to be published next week.
